senses: opportunity, facilities (the means of doing something)
la:noun:copia.html:
cōpĭa, ae, f.
co-ops
,
abundant power, wealth, riches, abundance (very freq. in all periods and species of composition).
Of material objects.
Of possessions, resources, wealth, supplies, riches, prosperity (syn.: divitiae, opes; opp. inopia): pro re nitorem et gloriam pro copiā,: divitiarum fructus in copiā est; copiam autem declarat satietas rerum et abundantia,; : copiis rei familiaris locupletes et pecuniosi,: utrum copiane sit agri, vectigalium, pecuniae, an penuria,: frugum,: publicani suas rationes et copias in illam provinciam contulerunt, id. Imp. Pomp.

7, 17: circumfluere omnibus copiis atque in omnium rerum abundantiā vivere, and 55; ; ; : Plenior ut si quos delectet copia justo,: Si recte frueris non est ut copia major Ab Jove donari possit tibi,; : exercitus omnium rerum abundabat copiā,: abundans omni copiā rerum est regio,: bonam copiam ejurare, to abjure property, i. e. to declare one's self exempt through poverty, .—Poet.: omnis copia narium ( = luxus odorum, Schol.),.—

In respect to other objects, fulness, copiousness, multitude, number, abundance: meretricum,: tanta copia venustatum aderat,: quorum (librorum) habeo Antii festivam copiam,: tanta copia virorum fortium atque innocentium,; cf.: tanta doctissimorum hominum, Dietsch: magna latronum in eā regione,: tubicinum,: procorum,: nimborum, et saep.—
In milit. lang. copia, and far more freq. in plur. copiae, ārum, men, troops, forces, army.
Sing.: omnis armatorum copia,: eā copiā, quam secum eduxit, se hanc civitatem oppressurum arbitratur,: ex omni copiā eligere aliquos,; ; Pompei. ap. , A, 3; Kritz; 61, 5.—
More freq. plur., orig. of a body of troops as made up of smaller bodies; cf. Engi. troops; the forces, troops, etc.: armare quam maximas copias,: copias secum adducere,; cf.: in angustum oppido nunc meae coguntur copiae,: cogere copias Brundusium, Cn. Pomp. ap. , A, 3; ; ; ; ; 1, 25; ; ; et saep.—
Of immaterial objects, fulness, copiousness, multitude, abundance.
In gen.: Quam tibi de quāvis unā re versibus omnis argumentorum sit copia missa per auris,: rerum copia verborum copiam gignit,; cf. rerum,; , prooem. § 1;: inventionis,: orationis,: sermonis,: abundare debet orator exemplorum copiā,: tanta facultas dicendi vel copia,: verborum,: in dicendo ubertas et copia,: dicendi,; ; ; and so of fulness in expression, absol., copia, ; ; : copias eloquentiae ponere in medio,: Platonis,: Senecae,.—
Esp., in reference to action, ability, power, might, opportunity, facilities, means of doing a thing.
With gen. gerund.: ut mi ejus facias conveniundi copiam,; so, facere,; cf. dare,; : edundi,: cunctandi,: illius inspectandi,: societatis amicitiaeque conjungendae,—
With inf.: quibus in otio vel magnifice vel molliter vivere copia erat,; so . —
With ut: cum copiam istam mihi et potestatem facis, ut ego, etc.,; ; —
Absol.: neque edepol facio: neque, si cupiam, copia est,; : ne quam aliam quaerat copiam ac te deserat,; cf. .—So pro copiā, according to one's ability, as one is able: volo habere hic aratiunculam pro copiā hic aput vos. : pro copiā supplicare Lari familiari,: dona pro copiā portantes,: in vehiculis pro copiā cujusque adornatīs,.—Esp. with the implication that one can do little: pro eā copiā quae Athenis erat, Sulp. ap. : pro rei copiā,: ludi funebres additi pro copiā provinciali et castrensi apparatu,: iudos pro temporis hujus copiā magnifici apparatus fecerunt,. —
Access to a person, with gen.: quando ejus copia est. ; cf.: obsecrat, ut sibi ejus faciat copiam,.

la:adj:copiosus.html:
cōpĭōsus, a, um, adj.
1. copia
.
Furnished abundantly with a thing, well supplied, having abundance, rich, copious, plentiful, abounding (in wealth, means of living, etc.) (very freq. and class., esp. in prose).
In gen.; constr. with abl., ab, or absol.; rarely with gen.
With simple abl. or ab and abl.: tu agris, tu aedificiis, tu argento, tu familiā, tu rebus omnibus ornatus et copiosus sis,: Arion grandi pecuniā et re bonā multā coplosus,: oppidum re cibariā,: Bruttedius artibus honestis,: locus a frumento,.—
Absol. (so most freq.): copiosa plane et locuples (mulier),: urbs,: via copiosa omniumque rerum abundans,; cf. stativa,: patrimonium,; : ingenium facile et copiosum,fertile in expedients, rich,: ratio loquendi,.—Comp.: provincia, Auct. B. Alex. 43. —Sup.: copiosissimum oppidum,: copiosissimus ac sollertissimus hostis, * : cucumeres,.—
With gen.: ager silvestrium caprarum,; cf. 1. copis. —
With ad: quamquam erat provincia minime copiosa ad alendos exercitus, Auct. B. Alex. 42.—
In partic., of an orator, or of discourse, rich in language, copious in expression, eloquent: homo copiosus ad dicendum,: lingua (opp. inops),: densior ille, hic copiosior in eloquendo,: oratores,: vir,: multa et varia et copiosa oratio,: loquacitas,; opp. jejunum,.—
Existing in rich abundance, copious (very rare): liquor putei,: varietas rerum abundat,: supellex verborum,.—Hence, cōpĭōsē, adv. (very freq.), in great abundance, copiously, abundantly, plentifully, copiously provided.
In gen.: sic copiose in provinciam profectus erat, ut, etc.,: large et copiose comparare pastum,: accepti tribus tricliniis,: senatorum urna copiose absolvit,by a large majority,: ornatus,.—
Esp., of discourse, copiously, fully, at length: copiose ab eo agri cultura laudatur,: copiose et abundanter loqui,: defendere causas reorum,: dicere,; .—Comp.: dicere,: haec omnia exsequi,.—Sup.: dicere,; ; : laudare,: defensum esse,: locus tractatur,.

la:verb:copulo.gloss: to bind or tie together, unite, join, couple
senses: to bind or tie together, unite, join, couple
la:verb:copulo.html:
cōpŭlo, āvi, ātum, 1 (
part. perf., contr. cōplata, ; dep. collat. form cō-pŭlor, āri, v. I. A. b. infra), v. a.
copula
, to couple, bind, or tie together, to join, connect, unite (class.; most freq. in Cic.).
Lit.
In gen.
With cum: hominem cum beluā,: caput et corpus cum aliquo,. —
With inter se: inter se quaedam possint coplata teneri,.—
With dat.: aurum auro,: utrimque Armeniae majori Sophene copulatur,.—
With ad: caput animalis ad pedem,.—(ε) With simple acc.: diversae insociabilesque arborum naturae copulantur,; .—
In dep. form: adeunt, consistunt, copulantur dexteras, Wagn. ad loc.; cf. ; , and P., and Ussing ad loc. (others explain dexteras as acc. of the part, or Gr. acc.).—
Esp., to confront: copulati in jus pervenimus,.—
Mid., to associate with: cave siris cum filiā meā copulari hanc,.—
Trop., to join, connect, unite.
With cum: sermonem cum aliquo,: futura cum praesentibus,: honestatem cum voluptate,: equestrem ordinem cum senatu,: se cum inimico,.—
With inter se: ah haec inter se jungi copularique possint?. 222.—
With dat.: quid naturae copulatum habuit Alcibiadis somnium?.—
With acc. only: libenter copulando verba jungebant, ut sodes pro si audes, etc.,; cf.: verba copulata (opp. simplicia),: constructio verborum tum conjunctionibus copuletur, tum dissolutionibus relaxetur,; ; cf. id. prooem. § 13: voluntates nostras,to unite,; cf. concordiam,: matrimonium, pr.; pr.; cf.: copulari matrimonio,; cf. ; and, taedis,.—Hence,
cōpŭlātus, a, um, P. a., joined together, united, connected: nihil est animis admixtum, nihil concretum, nihil copulatum, nihil coagmentatum, nihil duplex,: verba, v.supra, II. δ.—* Comp.: nihil amabilius nec copulatius quam morum similitudo bonorum,.—† Sup., Inscr. de Lyon, p. 477, 3.—Adv.: cōpŭlātē, connectedly (late Lat.): copulate dictum est (diequinti),; fin.—
cōpŭlātum, i, n., a joint sentence, the Gr. συμπεπλεγμένον, called also conjunctum, .

la:noun:copula.gloss: a bond, tie, band or other connecting item
senses: a bond, tie, band or other connecting item
la:noun:copula.html:
cōpŭla, ae (contr. form cōpla, in Wernsd. Poët. Lat. Min. IV. p. 535), f.
coapio
,
that which binds together or binds fast, a band, rope, thong, tie (rare; not in Cic.).
Lit.: tortae, ship's rigging, Att. ap. (Trag. Rel. v. 577 Rib.); : copulā vinctum ante se Thynem agere,; cf.: copula dura canem tenet,a leash,; ; : pectora copulae sparteae triturā continuā exulcerati (muli),, p. 224 fin.—Of the clasp of a bracelet, .—Of grapnel-hooks, etc., by which vessels were held in battle: eādem de causā minus commode copulis continebantur (naves), ex conj. (MSS. scopulis).—
Trop., a bond, tie, connection; of love: irrupta tenet,: nuptialis,; so, copula,; ; cf.: (Hymenaee), copula sacra deum, Kopp ad loc.—Of friendship: talium virorum,.—Of words, ; Nigid. ap. : ut dignitas eloquendi copulationis ipsius decore servetur,.

la:noun:copulatio.html:
cōpŭlātĭo, ōnis, f.
id.
,
a coupling, joining, connecting, uniting (several times in Cic. and Quint.).
Prop.: atomorum inter se (with complexiones and adhaesiones),; cf.: copulatio rerum et coagmentatio naturae,. —
Trop., of social union: primi congressus copulationesque,; cf. of marriage, Cod. Th. 9, 42, 2.—Of words: ordo rerum, et copulatio,; cf. : inoffensa vocum,: syllabarum, verborum inter se,.

the name of a plebeian family at Rome, e. g. the two brothers, T. and C. Coponii, ; .—Hence, Cōpōnĭānus, a, um, adj., of or pertaining to Coponius, .
